title: Multi-table, multi-statement transactions for the REST catalog
summary: Maninderjit Singh shared a consolidated proposal for multi-table, multi-statement transactions in the REST catalog, merging earlier proposals based on catalog-authored timestamps and sequence numbers. Dmitri Bourlatchkov asked for more attention to server-side impact and proposed opaque, catalog-managed commit IDs: the catalog returns a commit ID with each change, clients load other tables at that ID and pass it as the base of a multi-table commit, with no durable transaction context on the server. Jagdeep Sidhu noted that an earlier TransactionContext design with opaque IDs was dropped because it needed many catalog calls and server-side transaction state. Maninderjit agreed to add the option to the document and planned a meeting. In October 2026 Qiegang Long reported a proof of concept in Apache Polaris built on table branches and the existing multi-table commit, and asked whether the REST spec should define transactions or only the primitives catalogs need, such as an optional read-point parameter on loadTable. The thread has no replies to that question.

positions.stance: The consolidated proposal leaves server-side implementation to each vendor and asks which approach, catalog timestamps or sequence numbers, suits users.
Use commit IDs that are opaque to clients and resolved by the catalog, which needs REST API changes but no table spec change and no server-side transaction state.
The earlier TransactionContext approach with opaque IDs was dropped because it made the protocol chatty and required complex transaction state on the server.
The Iceberg REST spec should add minimal primitives, such as an opaque read point on loadTable, and leave higher-level transaction semantics to catalogs.

outcome.note: No decision was reached. A broader meeting was planned in 2025, and the questions raised with the Polaris proof-of-concept report in October 2026 have no replies in the thread.

why_it_matters: How multi-table transactions are exposed determines what catalog servers must implement and whether the REST spec gains transaction endpoints or only smaller primitives.
